The letter g in Samoan is the velar nasal [ŋ], the 'ng' of 'singer'.
The stressed syllable, with a clear, round o.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tah-ngah-LO-ah' — stress falls on the third syllable, and the g is a soft 'ng,' never a hard English g.

pronunciation.note: Tagaloa is single-tier Tier 2: the restoration adds no feature that plain ASCII loses — no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter — under the mechanical tier rule. The name's dignity is carried by its meaning, 'The Lord,' and by the scholarly consensus behind the restoration (Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; Craig 1989).

domains.title: Tagaloa
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Tagaloa is the supreme creator god of the Samoan islands, lord of the layered heavens who looked down on the empty sea and made the land. He is the maker of islands, the father of gods and chiefs, and the dweller in the highest sky — the figure around whom Samoan cosmology turns.

cards.name: Creator of the Isles
cards.desc: He threw down the vine and stone from which the Samoan islands were formed, founding the world itself.

cards.name: Lord of the Heavens
cards.desc: He dwells in Lani-uli, the highest of the layered heavens, above wind, rain, and the soaring birds.

cards.name: Father of Sina
cards.desc: His daughter Sina, mother of chiefs, anchors the island's greatest cycle of stories.

cards.name: Ocean's Lord
cards.desc: Across Polynesia his name is the sea's: Tangaroa in Aotearoa, Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Kanaloa in Hawai'i.

symbols.name: The Vine of the Isles
symbols.meaning: The heavenly vine Tagaloa let down into the sea, whose parts became the islands of Samoa

symbols.name: The Layered Heavens
symbols.meaning: Lani-uli and the descending storeys of the sky, his dwelling above all clouds

symbols.name: The Coconut Palm
symbols.meaning: Born from the body of the eel Tuna in the Sina cycle that belongs to Tagaloa's household

symbols.name: The Star-Path
symbols.meaning: In the wayfinding revival, the ocean road by which his dispersed namesakes are rejoined

mythology.lead: Tagaloa's mythology is cosmogony in the strict sense — stories of how land, people, and rank came to be. It survives not in epic but in creation chants recorded by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers, whose accounts disagree in detail but agree that the world began when the Lord of the Heavens acted upon the sea.

myths.title: The Vine Let Down into the Sea
myths.text: In the beginning Tagaloa dwelt alone in Lani-uli, the highest heaven, and beneath him lay only the boundless sea. He let down into the waters a vine from the sky; where its parts touched the surface, the islands of Samoa rose. On the largest he set the first settlement, and from the sky he watched over it. The fullest form of this creation account was recorded by the missionary J. B. Stair in Old Samoa (1897) and compared with related versions by Augustin Krämer in The Samoa Islands (1902); George Turner had published a shorter form in Nineteen Years in Polynesia (1861). Manu'a, the island group of the myth's first landing, is still styled the 'beginning of Samoa' in formal oratory, and the creation chant remained the deep charter for its paramount titles. The story is the charter of Samoan identity:The story is the charter of Samoan identity: the homeland is not discovered but made — thrown down from heaven and rooted in the sea.

myths.title: Sina and the Eel
myths.text: Tagaloa's daughter Sina came down to the pool of Mata o le Alelo to bathe, where a great eel, Tuna, confessed its love. When the eel was killed at Sina's command, she buried its head, and from it grew the first coconut palm — its two eyes, mouth, and body still showing on the nut. The tale was recorded across Polynesia (Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific, 1876; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology, 1970, §§ on the coconut cycle) and became the most retold of all Samoan stories. In Samoa the cycle carries a chiefly resonance as well: Sina's name became a byword for beauty in proverb, and her bathing pool, Mata o le Alelo, was pointed out to visitors into the twentieth century. The myth answers a child's questionThe myth answers a child's question — why does the coconut look like a face? — and binds the staple tree of island life to the death of an impossible love.

myths.title: The Storeys of the Sky
myths.text: Samoan cosmology stacks the sky into storeys — Lani-uli, Lani-ʻula, and the heavens beneath them — and places Tagaloa at the summit, above the winds that carry rain. Krämer (The Samoa Islands, 1902) recorded prayers addressing the ascending heavens by name, each storey ruled or traversed on the way to the Lord's seat. No text gives a complete, consistent map; the ethnographers themselves note that districts preserved different orders of the heavens. Below the storeys of the sky the same cosmology placed the underworld and the remote ends of the earth, and prayers were imagined to rise through the layers like visitors announced at the thresholds of a great chief's house. Yet the structure is constant:Yet the structure is constant: the sacred is vertical, and the higher the heaven, the nearer the Lord. Cosmology here is not speculation but orientation — the same layering a navigator reads in cloud and star.

myths.title: Tangaroa Driven to the Sea
myths.text: In the Māori version of the same divine name, Tangaroa is a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, the sky-father and earth-mother crushed in their parents' tight embrace. When Tāne thrust his parents apart to let in the light, Tangaroa fled to the ocean, and his enmity with Tāne — whose forests silt the sea — endures in myth (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 1855; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend, 1998). The Hawaiian Kanaloa and Tahitian Ta'aroa preserve further branches of the same god. Linguists reconstruct the shared ancestral form and read the god's names as a map of settlement itself — each island's dialect keeping its own office for the one Lord. Read across the ocean, the dispersalRead across the ocean, the dispersal of Tagaloa's name is itself the story: wherever Polynesians voyaged, the Lord went with them, changing office — creator in Samoa, sea-god in Aotearoa — but never name.

lore.syncretism: Christian missionaries arriving in Samoa in the 1830s found Tagaloa the principal rival of their God and absorbed rather than destroyed him: his title 'Atua' became the generic word for the Christian deity, and his mythology was pushed into folklore, where it survived. The pan-Polynesian evidence suggests an older unity: Tangaroa of Aotearoa, Ta'aroa of Tahiti, and Kanaloa of Hawai'i are cognate names with divergent portfolios, a pattern linguists explain by the settlement of the Pacific out of the Samoa–Tonga region (Tregear's comparative dictionary; Craig 1989). In Hawai'i, Kanaloa survives as the twin and companion of Kāne, the two wandering the islands together as culture-bringers — a pairing that arguably preserves Tagaloa's original creative role. In the twentieth century the Polynesian Voyaging Society's revival of long-distance navigation deliberately re-enshrined these sea-gods: Hōkūleʻa's ocean road was, in the crews' own framing, Tangaroa's and Kanaloa's road again.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tagaloa's most durable legacy is genealogical. Samoan orators trace chiefly lines (gafa) to divine ancestors of his household, and the sacred honorifics of chiefly oratory still invoke the sky's lordship. His daughter Sina gave her name to one of the most widespread of all Polynesian story-cycles — found from Samoa to Mangaia to Hawaii — and the proverbial Sina remains a figure of beauty and longing in Samoan speech. The god's name lives quietly in the landscape: villages, titles, and the old name Savai'i-region traditions. Since the 1970s the Pacific-wide voyaging renaissance has restored Tagaloa–Tangaroa–Kanaloa to active cultural memory: the canoe is again read as the sea-god's vehicle, and the navigator's art, once missionized into silence, is once more taught as his inheritance.
lore.extendedMeditation: What Tagaloa teaches is that creation can be an act of looking down. His world begins not with a battle or a body but with a lord in the highest heaven and an empty sea — and then a decision: to let something down. Polynesian cosmology is famously oceanic, yet its supreme god is a sky-dweller; the islands are the rope and bridge between the two. This is a theology suited to navigators: the world is made of layers — sky, sea, land, underworld — and authority flows along the vertical axis, from above downward, from the god to the chief to the people. Tagaloa is therefore less a 'god of' any one thing than the source of rank itself: where he acts, land appears; where his daughter descends, chiefs are born. To study him is to see how a non-literate society stored its constitution in cosmology, safe from conquest, until ethnographers wrote it down.
lore.archaeology: No cult image of Tagaloa is known — Samoan religion, like Polynesian religion generally, was essentially aniconic, and its temples were open-air malae and stone platforms rather than statue houses. The material landscape nevertheless preserves his world: Pulemelei mound on Savai'i, the largest prehistoric monument in Polynesia (roughly 60 × 50 m, dated by some researchers to the first millennium CE), served as a ceremonial platform, though which god it served is beyond proof. Scattered stone platforms, star mounds for pigeon-snaring (tia seu lupe), and chiefly burial sites across 'Upolu and Savai'i map the sacred geography the myths describe. The 'archaeology' of Tagaloa himself is documentary: the creation accounts recorded by Turner (1861), Stair (1897), Krämer (1902), and in the Journal of the Polynesian Society remain the primary evidence.
